content: Patients with end-stage kidney disease (ESKD) frequently develop anaemia, a condition often managed with erythropoiesis-stimulating agents (ESAs). These agents are used to maintain haemoglobin levels, thereby reducing the need for blood transfusions. However, approximately 5% to 10% of individuals with ESKD exhibit resistance to ESAs. Observational studies have indicated that patients requiring higher doses of ESAs face an increased risk of mortality. This review aimed to evaluate the effects of various interventions for treating ESA-resistant anaemia in individuals with ESKD. The researchers conducted a comprehensive search of databases, including the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL), MEDLINE, and EMBASE, to identify randomised controlled trials (RCTs) involving dialysis patients or pre-dialysis patients with stage 5 chronic kidney disease. The last search was conducted in April 2013. ESA resistance was defined as the inability to achieve or maintain target haemoglobin or haematocrit levels despite receiving appropriate doses of ESAs. Specifically, this included erythropoietin doses of ≥ 450 U/kg/week intravenously or ≥ 300 U/kg/week subcutaneously, or darbepoetin doses of ≥ 1.5 µg/kg/week, in patients without nutritional deficiencies or haematological/bleeding disorders. Broader criteria for ESA hyporesponsiveness included lower thresholds for erythropoietin (e.g., ≥ 300 U/kg/week intravenously or ≥ 200 U/kg/week subcutaneously) and darbepoetin (e.g., ≥ 1.0 µg/kg/week). Two independent reviewers assessed the quality of the studies and extracted data. Statistical analyses were performed using a random-effects model, with results expressed as risk ratios (RR) or mean differences (MD) alongside 95% confidence intervals (CI). Out of 521 records screened, 99 full-text articles were reviewed, but only two studies met the inclusion criteria. One study investigated the use of intravenous vitamin C compared to no additional treatment in 42 haemodialysis patients requiring high doses of intravenous erythropoietin (≥ 450 U/kg/week) over six months. The second study compared the use of high-flux dialysers versus low-flux dialysers in 48 haemodialysis patients requiring subcutaneous erythropoietin (≥ 200 U/kg/week) over six months. Due to the differences in interventions, the data from these studies could not be pooled for a quantitative meta-analysis. The authors concluded that there is insufficient evidence to recommend any specific intervention for improving ESA responsiveness in patients with ESKD. They emphasised the need for adequately powered RCTs to determine the safety and efficacy of potential treatments for ESA hyporesponsiveness.
